Task and constraints: Score a baseball game using integer rounds and operations C, D, and +.
Idea: Maintain a list of valid round scores and update it according to each operation.
Technique and why it applies: A numeric token appends a new score; D doubles the last score; + adds the previous two scores; C removes the last score. The final score is the sum of remaining rounds.
Invariant: temp contains the currently valid scores after processing each operation.
Edge cases: The code assumes C has a previous score and + has at least two scores. temp.remove(temp[-1]) removes the first equal value rather than necessarily the last occurrence, which can be wrong when duplicate scores exist.
Complexity: Each operation is O(1) except C's list.remove, which searches for the first matching value and can cost O(n); total worst-case time is O(n²), with O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the final baseball score from numeric entries and C, D, and + operations.
Idea: Use a stack-like history list, appending, doubling, summing, or popping scores as specified.
Technique and why it applies: The list's last entries represent the most recent valid rounds, so D reads the last score, + reads the last two, and C removes the last with pop().
Invariant: history stores the valid scores after all operations processed so far.
Edge cases: The input guarantees each operation is valid, so + and D have enough prior scores and C can pop safely.
Complexity: Each operation uses O(1) amortized list operations and the final sum is O(n), giving O(n) time and O(n) space. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Find the edge that creates a cycle in an undirected graph that was originally a tree.
Idea: Process edges in input order using a disjoint-set union structure; the first edge connecting vertices already in the same set is redundant.
Technique and why it applies: find follows parent links and compresses paths. union merges distinct components by rank and returns -1 when both endpoints already share a root.
Invariant: The disjoint-set structure represents connected components formed by previously processed edges.
Edge cases: Vertices are converted from 1-based labels to zero-based indices. UnionFind allocates parent and rank arrays of size len(vertex_set), which assumes labels are contiguous from 1 through that count, as guaranteed by the problem.
Complexity: With path compression and rank, operations are nearly O(1) amortized, so total time is O(n α(n)) and space O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Remove one directed edge so the remaining edges form a rooted tree with one parent per node.
Idea: Count indegrees, identify a node with two incoming edges if present, and use a disjoint-set structure to test candidate removals.
Technique and why it applies: When a node has two parents, one of its incoming edges must be removed; otherwise a cycle edge must be removed. DSU connectivity is used to detect whether the remaining edges still connect the candidate endpoints.
Invariant: count records indegree frequencies, and DSU tracks connectivity as edges are processed.
Edge cases: defaultdict is not imported in the shown code. isValidTree returns whether the endpoints of the skipped edge remain connected, which is a cycle check but does not by itself prove the whole directed graph is a rooted tree. The no-indegree-two branch may fall through without a return.
Complexity: The intended DSU approach is O(n α(n)) time and O(n) space, but the supplied implementation has correctness and missing-return issues. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of repetitions of A needed so B becomes a substring.
Idea: Handle the case where A is at least as long as B, then estimate repetitions using where A appears in B and the remaining length.
Technique and why it applies: If B is already inside A, one repetition suffices; if it is inside A*2, two suffice. Otherwise prefix and postfix lengths estimate how many copies span B, followed by a substring check.
Invariant: repeat is intended to be the smallest number of A copies long enough to cover B's required span.
Edge cases: B may straddle copy boundaries, which is why the final repeated-string check is necessary. B.find(A) returns -1 when A is absent, and max(0,...) converts that to zero, which can make the estimate incorrect for some inputs.
Complexity: String multiplication and membership checks can take O(|A|·repeat + |B|) time and memory. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Calculate the probability that a knight remains on an n-by-n chessboard after exactly k moves.
Idea: Memoize the survival probability from a cell and move count, averaging over the knight's eight possible moves.
Technique and why it applies: An off-board move contributes zero probability. At k moves, a still-on-board position contributes one; otherwise the method averages the recursive probabilities of all eight destinations.
Invariant: cache[(i,j,moves)] stores the probability of remaining on the board through the remaining moves from that state, under the method's move-count convention.
Edge cases: k=0 returns one for a valid starting cell. The code uses no probability normalization other than multiplying each branch by 1/8.
Complexity: There are O(k n²) states and eight transitions per state, giving O(k n²) time and O(k n²) memo space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the probability that a knight remains on the board after K moves from (r,c).
Idea: Use two DP layers, where each cell stores the probability of surviving the current number of moves when starting there.
Technique and why it applies: For each cell, sum one eighth of the previous layer's probabilities for all valid knight destinations. Two rows indexed by step parity reuse storage.
Invariant: dp[step%2][i][j] is the survival probability after step moves from cell (i,j).
Edge cases: K=0 returns the initialized value one for every cell. Out-of-board destinations contribute zero because they are not added.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(KN²) time and the two layers use O(N²) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Choose three non-overlapping length-k subarrays whose total sum is maximum, returning their starting indices.
Idea: Compute every window sum with prefix sums and memoize a recursive choice between taking the current window or skipping its start.
Technique and why it applies: Taking a window advances i by k to prevent overlap and decreases t; skipping advances i by one. The comparison selects the larger total, preferring taking on ties due to the strict less-than check.
Invariant: dfs(i,t) returns the maximum sum obtainable by choosing t windows from starts i onward, along with their indices.
Edge cases: The base case t=0 returns zero and an empty index list. If no valid set exists, negative infinity propagates; the problem guarantees enough elements for three windows.
Complexity: There are O(n·3) memo states and O(1) work per state aside from list concatenation, which can add O(3) per result; time is O(n) and cache/output space O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of stickers needed to spell target, where each sticker can be reused and letters can be rearranged.
Idea: Memoize recursion on the remaining target string, trying stickers that contain its first character.
Technique and why it applies: The first-letter filter avoids stickers that cannot reduce the current target. For each selected sticker, the code subtracts its character counts and recurses on the residual multiset encoded as a sorted alphabet string.
Invariant: dfs(target) is the minimum sticker count needed to cover the characters in the target argument.
Edge cases: An empty target returns zero. If no sticker contains the first target character, res remains infinity and the method returns -1. Repeated characters are represented by repeated letters in s.
Complexity: The state space can be exponential in target length, with each state testing all stickers and rebuilding strings. Memoization reduces repeated states but worst-case time and space remain exponential. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent words, ordering equal-frequency words lexicographically.
Idea: Count word occurrences, create heap entries with negative frequencies and word strings, then pop k entries.
Technique and why it applies: The min-heap prioritizes more frequent words because counts are negated. For equal counts, the string field sorts alphabetically, implementing the tie-break rule.
Invariant: The heap contains one pair per distinct word, and each pop yields the next word under frequency/lexical ordering.
Edge cases: k is assumed no greater than the number of distinct words. Heap construction uses one entry per unique word.
Complexity: Counting is O(n) expected time and heap construction/pop operations take O(u + k log u) for u distinct words; storage is O(u). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent words, breaking frequency ties by lexicographically smaller words first.
Idea: Count frequencies and maintain a size-k min-heap whose custom comparison keeps the least desirable candidate at the top.
Technique and why it applies: The heap holds at most k+1 entries; after each push, popping removes the lowest-ranked item. Popping the final heap and reversing the list yields the selected words in best-first order.
Invariant: After each distinct word is processed, the heap retains the best k words seen so far, aside from the temporary extra entry.
Edge cases: When fewer than k distinct words exist, the heap returns all of them. The custom __lt__ reverses lexical order for equal frequencies so the lexicographically larger word is removed first.
Complexity: Counting is O(n); heap operations are O(u log k), giving O(n+u log k) time and O(u) Counter storage plus O(k) heap. The author O(n log k) shorthand is reasonable.

Task and constraints: Find the k most frequent words with lexical ordering for frequency ties.
Idea: Bucket words by frequency, scan frequencies from highest to lowest, then sort the collected candidates by negative frequency and word.
Technique and why it applies: Each word is placed in a bucket indexed by its count. Scanning descending counts accumulates enough candidates; sorting pairs ensures frequency and alphabetical tie order.
Invariant: buckets[f] contains exactly the distinct words with frequency f, and pairs contains the highest-frequency candidates found so far.
Edge cases: The loop scans range(len(words)-1 down to zero), so a word occurring len(words) times is never visited in the bucket scan; this can omit a valid candidate in the all-identical case.
Complexity: Counting and bucketing take O(n), but sorting up to n candidates costs O(n log n); storage is O(n). The author time label is a broad bound.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent words, with alphabetical order resolving equal counts.
Idea: Count words, use randomized quickselect to partition by frequency/word tuple, then sort the first k selected pairs.
Technique and why it applies: Tuples (-count,word) rank higher frequencies first and lexical order second. kthElement partitions around a random pivot until the boundary rank k-1 is placed; sorting the first k entries establishes final order.
Invariant: After quickselect finishes, the first k tuples are the k best-ranked candidates, though not necessarily sorted among themselves.
Edge cases: The code assumes k is valid. The condition `i != k != j` is not used here; tuple ordering itself handles ties. Imports for collections.Counter are present.
Complexity: Randomized quickselect is expected O(u) but worst-case O(u²) for u distinct words, plus O(k log k) sorting; storage is O(u). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the binary representation of n alternates between zero and one at every adjacent position.
Idea: Convert n to its binary string and check every adjacent pair of characters.
Technique and why it applies: An alternating binary representation contains neither '00' nor '11'. The method returns False at the first equal adjacent pair and True if the scan completes.
Invariant: Every adjacent pair examined so far has different bits if the method continues.
Edge cases: A one-bit representation returns True because there are no adjacent pairs. n is assumed positive under the problem constraints.
Complexity: Binary conversion and scanning take O(log n) time and O(log n) space for the string. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether the binary digits of n alternate between zero and one.
Idea: Repeatedly divide by two, comparing each current least-significant bit with the previously extracted bit.
Technique and why it applies: divmod returns the quotient and current bit. If two consecutive extracted bits match, the representation is not alternating; otherwise the loop continues until all bits are consumed.
Invariant: curr is the previously extracted bit, and n contains the unprocessed higher-order bits.
Edge cases: n=1 returns True because the loop is skipped. The code assumes positive input; zero also returns True under its loop behavior.
Complexity: It processes one bit per iteration, so O(log n) time and O(1) space. The author O(1) time label assumes a fixed-width integer model.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum area of a connected island of land cells in a binary grid.
Idea: Scan every cell and run recursive DFS from each unvisited land cell, marking land as visited in the grid.
Technique and why it applies: DFS explores four-direction neighbors and adds one for each land cell reached. Replacing visited land with '#' prevents it from being counted again.
Invariant: Each DFS returns the area of one connected component, and maxArea stores the largest component area found.
Edge cases: Empty grid returns zero. The method mutates the grid by marking land. Recursion depth can be large for a long connected island.
Complexity: Each cell is visited once, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case recursion stack space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the size of the largest connected group of land cells.
Idea: Scan the grid and run DFS from each positive cell, marking visited land by negating its value.
Technique and why it applies: dfs rejects out-of-bounds or nonpositive cells, marks a land cell negative, increments the shared area counter, and recursively visits four neighbors.
Invariant: Negative grid values mark cells already included in an island, while area[0] counts the current DFS component.
Edge cases: The code mutates grid in place. Empty grid or empty first row is not explicitly handled and would fail when accessing grid[0].
Complexity: Each cell is visited once, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) recursion depth in the worst case. The author time label is correct; auxiliary space is not constant.

Task and constraints: Count substrings with equal consecutive runs of zeros and ones, where each run consists of one repeated bit.
Idea: Track the lengths of the previous and current runs and add their minimum whenever the bit changes.
Technique and why it applies: Every boundary between runs contributes min(previous_run,current_run) valid substrings because a substring can include equal-sized suffix/prefix portions of the adjacent runs.
Invariant: pre_cont_occ and cur_cont_occ store the lengths of the last completed run and current run.
Edge cases: A string with one run contributes zero because previous run length remains zero. The final min is added after the loop to count substrings ending at the last character.
Complexity: The string is scanned once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count binary substrings with equal numbers of consecutive zeros and ones, with each group contiguous.
Idea: Track previous and current run lengths and sum the smaller run at each transition.
Technique and why it applies: A valid substring can take the same number of characters from the end of one run and start of the next, so each pair of adjacent runs contributes the minimum of their lengths.
Invariant: prev is the completed run length immediately before curr, and result sums contributions from all processed run boundaries.
Edge cases: A one-character string returns zero. The final addition accounts for the last pair of runs after the scan ends.
Complexity: The algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray whose set of values has the same degree as the full array.
Idea: Group indices by value, find the maximum frequency, then minimize the first-to-last span among values with that frequency.
Technique and why it applies: The degree is the largest count of any value. For each value achieving that count, its shortest covering interval runs from its first occurrence to its last occurrence.
Invariant: d[value] contains all occurrence indices for that value, and best is the smallest span found among maximum-frequency values.
Edge cases: defaultdict is referenced but not imported in the shown snippet. A single distinct value gives the full array length as the shortest span.
Complexity: Building index lists and scanning them takes O(n) time and O(n) space. No labels were supplied.
